content:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is treated with disease-modifying medicines called DMARDs, which calm the immune system and help prevent joint damage. Treatment should start as early as possible, ideally soon after diagnosis by a rheumatologist. The aim is remission or very low disease activity, and many people now reach it. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and self-care support the medicines.

Why early treatment matters

RA is an autoimmune condition. The immune system attacks the lining of the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. Without treatment this inflammation can damage joints permanently. NICE (NG100) recommends that adults with suspected persistent synovitis are referred urgently to rheumatology and that treatment begins as soon as possible after diagnosis.

Related reading: What Is Rheumatoid Arthritis?, Best Exercise for Rheumatoid Arthritis, Arthritis Treatment — Your Complete Guide to Managing Joint Pain

The main medicines

Conventional DMARDs. NICE recommends starting with one of these, usually methotrexate. Leflunomide or sulfasalazine are alternatives, and hydroxychloroquine may be used for milder disease. They take several weeks to months to work fully, so it is important to keep taking them even if you do not notice a change straight away.

Short-term steroids. A short course of steroid tablets or an injection may be given to control symptoms quickly while DMARDs start working. NICE advises keeping steroid use as short as possible because of long-term side effects.

Biologic and targeted medicines. If DMARDs do not control the disease well enough, you may be offered a biologic medicine, such as an anti-TNF, or a JAK inhibitor tablet. On the NHS these are offered when disease activity reaches the level set out by NICE.

Pain relief. Painkillers and anti-inflammatory medicines help symptoms but do not change the disease. Your GP or pharmacist will advise on safe use, especially with other medicines.

Treat to target

Your team will measure how active your RA is, often using a score called DAS28. This combines joint counts, blood tests and how you feel. Treatment is adjusted until you reach the target. NICE suggests monthly reviews until the disease is controlled, then an annual review.

Monitoring and safety

DMARDs and biologics need regular blood tests to check blood counts, liver and kidney function. Keep these appointments, as they help catch side effects early. Your team will also advise on:

  • infections: some treatments make infections more likely. Report fever or feeling unwell promptly.
  • vaccines: flu, COVID-19 and pneumonia vaccines are usually recommended. Some live vaccines may not be suitable.
  • pregnancy: some medicines must be stopped well before trying to conceive. Discuss plans early.
  • alcohol: limits apply with methotrexate. Ask your team what is safe for you.

Physiotherapy, OT and podiatry

NICE recommends access to a multidisciplinary team. A physiotherapist can help with exercise to keep joints moving and muscles strong. An occupational therapist can advise on hand function, splints, equipment and work. A podiatrist can help with foot problems, which are common in RA.

What you can do yourself

  • Stay active. Regular exercise reduces stiffness and fatigue and protects your heart.
  • Stop smoking. Smoking makes RA more active and can reduce how well treatment works.
  • Look after your heart. RA raises cardiovascular risk. Have your blood pressure and cholesterol checked.
  • Pace yourself and plan rest around busy days.
  • Learn your flare plan. Ask your team who to contact if your joints become more swollen.

Living with RA day to day

Fatigue is common in RA and can be as hard to live with as pain. It often improves as inflammation is controlled, but pacing, regular gentle exercise and good sleep habits also help. Low mood and anxiety are common too, and talking therapies are available on the NHS through self-referral in England.

If work is getting harder, you may be entitled to reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010, and Access to Work can help with equipment or travel costs. Benefits such as Personal Independence Payment may be available depending on how RA affects your daily life.

If treatment is not working

Tell your team if you still have swollen joints, long morning stiffness or side effects. There are many treatment options, and switching is common. Most people find a combination that works for them.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
